meta.name: GetHired Quick Knowledge Check — Question Bank
meta.note: Lighter-weight MCQ companion to the full scenario-based practical assessment. Rule-based grading only (exact choice-id match) — no AI. Covers the same actionable categories as the CV corpus (education excluded).
meta.role_gating_note: V4-P3 added a `roles` array to every question, gated by real relevance rather than category exclusion (unlike the Practical Assessment's investigation-domain categories, MCQ's categories — certifications/tools/concepts/scripting/soft-skills — are all cross-cutting corpus categories every role touches, per data/corpus.json's own per-role weighting). Grounded in corpus.json's existing researched per-role weights for the same real-world items each question tests (e.g. Nmap: vapt 9 / netsec 5 / soc 3 -> gated to vapt+netsec, not soc; CEH: vapt 8 / soc 5 / netsec 2 -> gated to vapt+soc, not netsec) using a >=5-weight inclusion threshold, plus a couple of items kept universal where the underlying concept is genuinely foundational regardless of track (Security+, CIA triad, Wireshark, Bash, documentation practice) rather than forcing an artificial split. generalist always sees every question. Every role sees at least one question per category.
meta.role_specificity_note: A later pass found the original per-role split was mostly the same generic skill-category questions with a role tag, not questions that actually test what each role does — added real role-differentiated content grounded in the same fresher-job-posting research used for the Practical Assessment: vapt gained offensive-reasoning questions (Burp Suite usage, SQLi pattern recognition, OWASP category mapping, OSCP), soc_analyst gained defensive/monitoring questions (SIEM brute-force correlation, alert-triage judgment on a scheduled scan false positive, incident-response phase ordering, an EDR process-tree finding), and network_security_engineer gained infra-config questions (a least-privilege firewall misconfiguration, IDS vs. IPS, VPN concentrators, subnetting, CCNA). generalist includes all of it, matching its broad-mix positioning; existing shared/foundational questions were left as-is.
meta.cross_track_dedup_note: That pass still left 8 questions (cert-1, cert-2, tools-1, tools-2, concepts-1, script-1, script-2, soft-1) literally identical — same wording, same choices — across two or three of soc_analyst/vapt/network_security_engineer, which isn't allowed even when the underlying topic is legitimately shared (generalist overlapping with all three is fine and intentional; the three specific tracks overlapping with each other is not). Each was reassigned to sole ownership by one track (cert-1/Security+ and tools-1/Wireshark to soc_analyst; cert-2/CEH, tools-2/Nmap, concepts-1/CIA-triad, script-2/Python to vapt; script-1/Bash to network_security_engineer), and 13 new track-specific replacement questions were added so no track's total question count decreased: soc_analyst gained cert-5 (CySA+), concepts-10 (dwell time), script-4 (log-filtering), script-5 (scripting motivation); vapt gained cert-6 (eJPT), tools-7 (Metasploit), script-3 (Python for pentest tooling), soft-3 (report-writing); network_security_engineer gained cert-7 (PCNSA), tools-8 (network monitoring), tools-9 (ping), concepts-11 (DMZ), soft-4 (change management). Per-track totals before/after this pass: soc_analyst 12/12, vapt 13/13, network_security_engineer 11/11 — same count, zero cross-track duplication remaining.

questions.question: Which certification is most commonly cited as a foundational, vendor-neutral entry point into cybersecurity roles?
questions.explanation: CompTIA Security+ is widely used as a baseline entry-level cert — CISSP and OSCP both expect prior experience, and CCIE is a advanced networking cert, not a security fundamentals one.

questions.question: What does CEH stand for?
questions.explanation: CEH (Certified Ethical Hacker) is an EC-Council certification focused on offensive-security fundamentals.

questions.question: Which certification is widely regarded as the industry benchmark for hands-on penetration testing skill, requiring candidates to compromise machines in a timed practical exam?
questions.explanation: OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional) is known specifically for its hands-on, timed practical exam — you have to actually compromise machines, not just answer multiple-choice questions.

questions.question: Which certification path is most associated with entry-level network security and firewall administration roles?
questions.explanation: Cisco's CCNA (and the security-focused CCNA Security) is the standard entry point for network infrastructure and firewall/routing roles — OSCP and CEH lean offensive, and CIPP is a privacy-law certification, not a technical one.

questions.question: Which certification specifically validates practical security-operations and SOC-analyst skills, beyond a general security fundamentals cert?
questions.explanation: CompTIA CySA+ (Cybersecurity Analyst+) is specifically aimed at SOC-style skills — behavioral analytics, threat detection, and incident response — a step beyond the more general Security+.

questions.question: Which certification is specifically designed as an entry-level, hands-on penetration testing credential, often recommended as a stepping stone before OSCP?
questions.explanation: eJPT is built specifically for beginners breaking into penetration testing, with a practical (not just multiple-choice) exam format — commonly recommended as a first hands-on cert before tackling OSCP.

questions.question: Which certification focuses specifically on firewall and security-appliance administration from a leading network security vendor?

choices.label: PCNSA (Palo Alto Networks Certified Network Security Administrator)

questions.explanation: PCNSA validates hands-on administration of Palo Alto Networks firewalls specifically — a concrete, vendor-backed credential distinct from broader networking certs like CCNA.

questions.question: Which tool is primarily used for capturing and analyzing network packets?
questions.explanation: Wireshark captures and inspects live network traffic at the packet level — Nmap is for scanning, Metasploit for exploitation, and Burp Suite for web app testing.

questions.question: Nmap is most commonly used for which purpose?

choices.label: Editing HTTP requests in a proxy

questions.explanation: Nmap's core purpose is discovering hosts and open ports on a network — a standard first step in both offensive and defensive reconnaissance.

questions.question: You're testing a web application for injection vulnerabilities and need to intercept and modify HTTP requests in real time before they reach the server. Which tool is built for this?
questions.explanation: Burp Suite is the standard intercepting proxy for capturing and modifying HTTP requests/responses during web app pentesting — Nmap is for scanning, Wireshark for packet capture, Splunk for log aggregation.

questions.question: A SIEM correlation rule fires because a single user account failed login 50 times in one minute from the same IP, then succeeded. What should this pattern be flagged as?
questions.explanation: Dozens of rapid failed logins followed by a success from one source is the signature shape of a brute-force attack — exactly what SIEM correlation rules are built to catch.

questions.question: An EDR tool flags a process tree where Microsoft Word spawned PowerShell, which then made an outbound connection to an unfamiliar IP. What should this be treated as?

choices.label: Normal Office functionality, no action needed
A likely malicious macro / initial-access chain requiring investigation

questions.explanation: Office applications legitimately have no reason to spawn a shell — Word launching PowerShell, which then reaches out to the internet, is a well-known red flag for a malicious macro delivering a second-stage payload.

questions.question: Which device or technology would you configure to give remote employees encrypted access into the corporate network over the public internet?
questions.explanation: A VPN concentrator terminates and manages encrypted remote-access tunnels — load balancers distribute traffic, DNS resolves names, and a WAF filters web app traffic, none of which provide remote-access encryption.

questions.question: Which tool would you use to identify and exploit a known vulnerability on a target automatically, matching it to a pre-built exploit module?
questions.explanation: Metasploit is the standard exploitation framework for matching known vulnerabilities to ready-made exploit modules and payloads — Wireshark and Splunk are for traffic/log analysis, not exploitation.

questions.question: Which type of tool would you use to visually map and continuously monitor the health of your network's routers, switches, and links?

choices.label: A network monitoring/mapping tool (e.g. SolarWinds, PRTG)

questions.explanation: Network monitoring platforms like SolarWinds or PRTG give continuous visibility into device and link health — the other options are offensive-testing or credential tools, not infrastructure monitoring.

questions.question: Which simple tool/protocol would you check first to confirm basic Layer 3 reachability between two devices, before troubleshooting anything more complex?
questions.explanation: A basic ping confirms whether two devices can reach each other at all at Layer 3 — the cheapest, fastest first check before digging into packet captures or anything more involved.

questions.question: In the CIA triad, what does the 'C' stand for?
questions.explanation: The CIA triad is Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability — the three core properties information security aims to protect.

questions.question: Which OWASP Top 10 (2021) category covers classic SQL injection?
questions.explanation: SQL injection is a canonical example of the OWASP 'Injection' category (A03:2021), which covers untrusted input being interpreted as code by an interpreter.

questions.question: A tester submits ' OR '1'='1 into a login field and gains access without valid credentials. What attack pattern does this describe?
questions.explanation: This is the classic SQL injection auth-bypass payload — the always-true condition ' OR '1'='1 manipulates the login query's logic to succeed regardless of the actual password.

questions.question: An application uses a JavaScript library with a publicly disclosed critical vulnerability from several years ago, and the dev team never updated it. Which OWASP Top 10 (2021) category covers this?

choices.label: A09:2021 – Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

questions.explanation: Using components with known, unpatched vulnerabilities is exactly what OWASP's A06:2021 – Vulnerable and Outdated Components category covers.

questions.question: An analyst receives an alert that a known internal vulnerability scanner triggered an IDS signature for port scanning, during its regular scheduled scan window. How should this alert be triaged?

choices.label: False positive — expected, scheduled scanning activity

questions.explanation: Recognizing expected, authorized activity (like a scheduled internal vuln scan) versus genuine malicious activity is core to alert triage — this closes as a known false positive, not an incident.

questions.question: Which of these is the correct order of the standard incident response lifecycle, day to day?
questions.explanation: You have to detect an incident before you can contain it, contain it before removing the threat (eradication), and eradicate before restoring normal operations (recovery).

questions.question: A firewall denies all inbound traffic by default, but an admin added an ALLOW ANY ANY rule on port 3389 for troubleshooting and forgot to remove it. What security principle does this violate?
questions.explanation: Leaving a wide-open ANY ANY rule active grants far more access than needed for troubleshooting — the opposite of least privilege, which says access should be scoped to only what's necessary.

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between an IDS and an IPS?

choices.label: An IDS only monitors and alerts; an IPS can actively block or drop malicious traffic in-line
An IDS works only at Layer 2; an IPS works only at Layer 7
They're marketing terms for the same product with no real difference
An IDS is hardware-only; an IPS is software-only

questions.explanation: An IDS is passive — it detects and alerts. An IPS sits in-line with traffic and can actively block or drop malicious packets in real time — the detect-vs-block distinction is the actual difference, not the layer or hardware/software form factor.

questions.question: A host has the IP 172.16.0.10/28. How many usable host addresses exist in this subnet?
questions.explanation: A /28 has 16 total addresses; subtract 2 for the network and broadcast addresses, leaving 14 usable host addresses.

questions.question: What does 'dwell time' refer to in the context of a security incident?

choices.label: How long an attacker remains undetected in an environment before being found
How long a SOC shift lasts
How long a ticket sits unassigned in the queue
How long a password remains valid before rotation

questions.explanation: Dwell time — the gap between initial compromise and detection/containment — is a widely-cited metric in threat reports, and a big part of why fast detection matters as much as prevention.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a DMZ (demilitarized zone) in network architecture?

choices.label: An isolated network segment for public-facing services, separate from the internal network
A backup power supply for network equipment

questions.explanation: A DMZ hosts public-facing services (web servers, mail relays, etc.) in an isolated segment, so that if one of those services is compromised, the attacker doesn't land directly on the internal network.

questions.question: Which language is most commonly used for quick automation scripts directly in a Linux terminal?
questions.explanation: Bash is the default shell scripting language on most Linux systems, ideal for quick automation without a compile step.

questions.question: What file extension does a Python script typically use?
questions.explanation: Python source files use the .py extension.

questions.question: Which scripting language is most commonly used to write quick custom exploit or automation scripts during a pentest, due to its large security-tooling ecosystem (e.g. Scapy, requests, pwntools)?
questions.explanation: Python's huge security-focused library ecosystem (Scapy for packet crafting, requests for HTTP, pwntools for exploit dev) makes it the default glue language for custom pentest tooling.

questions.question: A SOC analyst wants to pull the last hour of failed-login events from a large log file and count occurrences per source IP, without doing it by hand. What kind of solution fits best?

choices.label: A short script or SIEM search query to filter and count automatically
Manually scrolling through the raw file
Emailing the vendor to ask them to check

questions.explanation: A short script or search query (grep/awk, a SIEM query language, or a quick Python pass) is the practical, repeatable way to do this — manual scrolling doesn't scale past a handful of lines.

questions.question: Why might a SOC analyst learn basic Python or PowerShell scripting, even in a role that's mostly about monitoring alerts?

choices.label: To automate repetitive investigation/enrichment steps across tools
Scripting is strictly required to get hired at any SOC
It has no real use in a SOC role

questions.explanation: Basic scripting lets an analyst automate the repetitive parts of investigation — pulling context on an IP or file hash across multiple tools, for example — instead of doing the same manual lookups on every alert.

questions.question: Why is clear documentation especially important during incident response?

choices.label: It's only required for legal teams
It slows the response down unnecessarily
It enables handoff between analysts and creates an audit trail

questions.explanation: Good documentation lets an incident be handed off between shifts or analysts without losing context, and creates a record for post-incident review.

questions.question: Which of these best describes 'attention to detail' in a SOC analyst context?

choices.label: Working as fast as possible regardless of accuracy
Noticing subtle anomalies in logs or alerts that automated tools might miss
Only escalating alerts already marked critical
Ignoring low-severity alerts to save time

questions.explanation: Automated tools flag known patterns — an analyst's attention to detail is what catches the subtle, unusual signal that doesn't match a pre-built rule.

questions.question: Why is clear, well-organized report writing considered as important as the technical exploitation work in a pentest engagement?

choices.label: Because the report is what the client actually acts on to fix issues
Reports are just a formality nobody reads
Reports are optional if the engagement went well

questions.explanation: A client's developers and management act on the written report, not on what happened during testing — a technically brilliant finding that's poorly explained often just doesn't get fixed.

questions.question: Why is careful change management (documenting and scheduling firewall/network changes) especially important in network security work?

choices.label: An undocumented or poorly-planned change can cause outages or security gaps affecting many users at once
Documentation slows down urgent fixes and should be skipped
Only major changes need any review
Change management is only relevant to software developers

questions.explanation: A single misconfigured firewall or routing change can take down critical services or open a serious gap, often affecting an entire organization at once — disciplined change management is how that risk gets caught before it ships.
